claim: The study constructed an atlas of associations between 125 different PGS derived using results from genome-wide association studies and 249 circulating metabolites in up to 83,004 participants from the UK Biobank.
source: We sought to construct an atlas of associations between 125 different PGS derived using results from genome-wide association studies and 249 circulating metabolites in up to 83,004 participants from the UK Biobank.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of PGS (125), metabolites (249), and participants (83,004) analyzed.

claim: GlycA is an inflammatory biomarker.
source: As an exemplar to demonstrate the value of this atlas, we conducted a hypothesis-free evaluation of all associations with glycoprotein acetyls (GlycA), an inflammatory biomarker.
evidence: The manuscript directly describes GlycA as an inflammatory biomarker.

claim: The associations between GlycA and various PGS likely reflect the effect of risk factors, such as adiposity or liability towards smoking, on systemic inflammation rather than the converse direction.
source: Using bidirectional Mendelian randomization, we find that the associations highlighted likely reflect the effect of risk factors, such as adiposity or liability towards smoking, on systemic inflammation as opposed to the converse direction.
evidence: The claim is supported by bidirectional Mendelian randomization analyses conducted in the study.

claim: All results can be visualized and downloaded at http://mrcieu.mrsoftware.org/metabolites_PRS_atlas.
source: All results can be visualized and downloaded at http://mrcieu.mrsoftware.org/metabolites_PRS_atlas.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the URL for accessing the results.

claim: Complex traits and disease have a polygenic architecture meaning that they are influenced by many genetic variants scattered throughout the human genome.
source: Complex traits and disease have a polygenic architecture meaning that they are influenced by many genetic variants scattered throughout the human genome (Boyle et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Boyle et al., 2017.

claim: Polygenic scores have emerged as powerful tools for predicting lifelong risk of disease.
source: In the last decade, PGS have emerged as powerful tools for predicting lifelong risk of disease, which is predominantly due to the dramatic increase in sample sizes of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and their continued success in uncovering trait-associated genetic variants across the genome (Visscher et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Visscher et al., 2017.

claim: PGS have utility in a causal inference setting to establish causal effects between risk factors and disease outcomes.
source: Additionally, PGS have utility in a causal inference setting to establish causal effects between risk factors and disease outcomes, as well as to help elucidate putative diagnostic and prognostic biomarkers for disease incidence (Richardson et al., 2019b, Holmes and Davey Smith, 2019; Ritchie et al., 2021a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Richardson et al., 2019b, Holmes and Davey Smith, 2019, and Ritchie et al., 2021a.

claim: The human metabolome consists of over 100,000 small molecules.
source: The human metabolome consists of over 100,000 small molecules and is a rich source of potential risk factors and biomarkers, as well as therapeutic targets (Holmes et al., 2021), for complex traits and disease (Gallois et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Holmes et al., 2021 and Gallois et al., 2019.

claim: Many circulating metabolic traits studied to date have a large heritable component as demonstrated by GWAS endeavours.
source: Many circulating metabolic traits studied to date have a large heritable component as demonstrated by GWAS endeavours (Suhre et al., 2011; Shin et al., 2014; MacTel Consortium et al., 2021), suggesting that they have a polygenic architecture.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Suhre et al., 2011, Shin et al., 2014, and MacTel Consortium et al., 2021.

claim: In-depth molecular profiling has recently been undertaken in the UK Biobank study using nuclear magnetic resonance to capture measures of 249 circulating metabolites in approximately 120,000 participants who also have genotype data.
source: In-depth molecular profiling has recently been undertaken in the UK Biobank (UKB) study using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) to capture measures of 249 circulating metabolites in approximately 120,000 participants who also have genotype data (Julkunen et al., 2021; Sudlow et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Julkunen et al., 2021 and Sudlow et al., 2015.

claim: The 249 metabolite measurements include the particle concentration, size, and composition of 14 lipoprotein subclasses, as well as the levels of phospholipids, fatty acids, amino acids, ketone bodies, and other biomarkers.
source: The 249 metabolite measurements include the particle concentration, size, and composition of 14 lipoprotein subclasses, as well as the levels of phospholipids, fatty acids, amino acids, ketone bodies, and other biomarkers as discussed in a recent review (Ala-Korpela et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ala-Korpela et al., 2022.

claim: Evaluations using PGS will likely yield higher statistical power than conventional observational associations for diseases with low prevalence in UK Biobank.
source: For example, as UKB is a prospective cohort study many diseases have low prevalence, such as Alzheimer's disease which typically has a late onset. In contrast, evaluations using PGS will likely yield higher statistical power given that a continuous genetic score will be analysed for all participants in UKB based on their liability to disease.
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning based on the continuous nature of PGS versus binary disease status.

claim: Mendelian randomization can be used to investigate whether a causal relationship may underlie findings.
source: We demonstrate the usefulness of this atlas in terms of highlighting putative risk factors and biomarkers for disease risk and advocate the use of an approach known as Mendelian randomization (MR) to investigate whether a causal relationship may underlie findings (Supplementary Note 2) (Davey Smith and Ebrahim, 2003, Davey Smith and Hemani, 2014; Sanderson et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Davey Smith and Ebrahim, 2003, Davey Smith and Hemani, 2014, and Sanderson et al., 2022.

claim: All PGS analyses were conducted in the full UKB sample, as well as in sex-stratified samples and age tertiles to evaluate the influence of medication use on findings.
source: Furthermore, all PGS analyses were initially conducted in the full UKB sample, as well as in sex-stratified samples and age tertiles as proposed previously to evaluate the influence of medication use on findings (Bell et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript describes the stratification approach with a citation to Bell et al., 2022.

claim: Age-dependent stratification allows comparisons between the youngest and oldest tertiles in UKB where the level of medication use is likely to vary between groups.
source: As the age of individuals in UKB is unlikely to induce sources of biases into analyses (e.g. collider bias), age-dependent stratification allows comparisons between the youngest and oldest tertiles in UKB where the level of medication use is likely to vary between groups.
evidence: The manuscript explains the rationale for age stratification.

claim: Stratification on medication use would introduce collider bias.
source: Stratification on medication use, by contrast, would introduce collider bias.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a methodological consideration.

claim: The majority of GWAS summary statistics were obtained from the OpenGWAS platform.
source: The majority of these summary statistics were obtained from the OpenGWAS platform and encompassed traits and disease outcomes from across the human phenome (Elsworth et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the source of GWAS data with a citation to Elsworth et al., 2020.

claim: GWAS were identified based on those conducted in populations of European descent.
source: GWAS were identified based on those conducted in populations of European descent given that our analysis in UKB was based on the European subset with NMR data.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the selection criteria for GWAS.

claim: Studies which did not include the UKB in their study were identified to avoid overlapping samples between PGS construction and analysis with metabolic traits.
source: Furthermore, we identified studies which did not include the UKB in their study to avoid overlapping samples between PGS construction and analysis with metabolic traits.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this selection criterion.

claim: Two versions of each PGS were built using different thresholds for variant-trait associations and linkage disequilibrium.
source: Two versions of each PGS were built using different thresholds for variant-trait associations (P) and linkage disequilibrium (LD; r2). These were (1) 'lenient' thresholds of p < 0.05 and r2 < 0.1 and (2) a 'stringent' threshold of p < 5 × 10−8 and r2 < 0.001.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the two PGS construction approaches.

claim: PGS were generated using the software PLINK.
source: PGS were generated using the software PLINK (Chang et al., 2015) with LD being calculated using a reference panel of 10,000 randomly selected unrelated UKB individuals of European descent (Kibinge et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the software used with citations to Chang et al., 2015 and Kibinge et al., 2020.

claim: The final sample size of n = 83,004 was determined based on individuals with both genotype and circulating metabolites data after removing participants with withdrawn consent, evidence of genetic relatedness or who were not of 'white European ancestry' based on a K-means clustering.
source: Our final sample size of n = 83,004 was determined based on individuals with both genotype and circulating metabolites data after removing participants with withdrawn consent, evidence of genetic relatedness or who were not of 'white European ancestry' based on a K-means clustering (K = 4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the sample selection process.

claim: All PGS were standardized to have a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1.
source: All PGS were standardized to have a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1 and similarly all metabolites were subject to inverse rank normalization transformations prior to analysis allowing cross-PGS/metabolite comparisons to be made.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the standardization procedure.

claim: All metabolites were subject to inverse rank normalization transformations prior to analysis.
source: All PGS were standardized to have a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1 and similarly all metabolites were subject to inverse rank normalization transformations prior to analysis allowing cross-PGS/metabolite comparisons to be made.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the normalization procedure.

claim: Analyses were conducted using linear regression adjusting for age, sex, and the top 10 principal components.
source: Analyses were conducted using linear regression adjusting for age, sex, and the top 10 principal components (PCs).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the statistical analysis approach.

claim: A web application was developed to query and visualize metabolic signatures for a given PGS.
source: To disseminate all findings from this large-scale analysis we have developed a web application (http://mrcieu.mrsoftware.org/metabolites_PRS_atlas/) to query and visualize metabolic signatures for a given PGS.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the web application.

claim: PC analysis suggested that the first 19 PCs captured 95% of the variance in the NMR metabolites data.
source: PC analysis suggested that the first 19 PCs captured 95% of the variance in the NMR metabolites data (whereas the first ten PCs captured 90% and the first 41 PCs captured 99% of the variance) (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the results of PC analysis.

claim: A heuristic of p < 0.05/19 was applied in this manuscript to account for multiple testing of the associations between any single PGS and the NMR metabolic traits.
source: We therefore have applied a heuristic of p < 0.05/19 in this manuscript to account for multiple testing of the associations between any single PGS and the NMR metabolic traits for downstream analyses, although users are able to download the full results to apply whatever correction they see fit.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the multiple testing correction approach.

claim: A false discovery rate of less than 0.05 calculated from the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure was applied to correct for multiple testing for all other analyses.
source: For all other analyses (e.g. associations between metabolic traits and all PGS), we apply a false discovery rate (FDR) of less than 0.05 calculated from the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to correct for multiple testing.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the FDR correction approach.

claim: There were a total of 5445 associations between PGS derived based on 'lenient criteria' in the full sample and NMR-assessed circulating metabolic traits based on the FDR threshold of 0.05.
source: Based on the FDR threshold of 0.05, there were a total of 5445 associations between PGS derived (derived based on 'lenient criteria' with p < 0.05 variants) in the full sample and NMR-assessed circulating metabolic traits.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the number of significant associations.

claim: The PGS with the largest number of associations robust to multiple testing corrections was body mass index (n = 217).
source: The PGS with the largest number of associations robust to multiple testing corrections was body mass index (BMI) (n = 217) (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this finding.

claim: VLDL particle average diameter size was associated with the PGS for BMI (Beta = 0.04, 95% CI = 0.033 to 0.046, p = 3.53 × 10−35).
source: For example, we applied MR to further evaluate associations highlighted in our atlas with VLDL particles, where both VLDL particle average diameter size and concentration were associated with the PGS for BMI (Beta = 0.04, 95% CI = 0.033 to 0.046, p = 3.53 × 10−35 and Beta = 0.012, 95% CI = 0.006 to 0.019, p = 2.7 × 10–4, respectively)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this association with statistical details.

claim: VLDL particle concentration was associated with the PGS for BMI (Beta = 0.012, 95% CI = 0.006 to 0.019, p = 2.7 × 10–4).
source: For example, we applied MR to further evaluate associations highlighted in our atlas with VLDL particles, where both VLDL particle average diameter size and concentration were associated with the PGS for BMI (Beta = 0.04, 95% CI = 0.033 to 0.046, p = 3.53 × 10−35 and Beta = 0.012, 95% CI = 0.006 to 0.019, p = 2.7 × 10–4, respectively)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this association with statistical details.

claim: VLDL particle average diameter size was associated with the coronary heart disease PGS (Beta = 0.026, 95% CI = 0.019 to 0.032, p = 2.12 × 10–15).
source: For example, we applied MR to further evaluate associations highlighted in our atlas with VLDL particles, where both VLDL particle average diameter size and concentration were associated with the PGS for BMI (Beta = 0.04, 95% CI = 0.033 to 0.046, p = 3.53 × 10−35 and Beta = 0.012, 95% CI = 0.006 to 0.019, p = 2.7 × 10–4, respectively) and also coronary heart disease (CHD) liability (Beta = 0.026, 95% CI = 0.019 to 0.032, p = 2.12 × 10–15 and Beta = 0.035, 95% CI = 0.028 to 0.042, p = 2.73 × 10–24, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this association with statistical details.

claim: VLDL particle concentration was associated with the coronary heart disease PGS (Beta = 0.035, 95% CI = 0.028 to 0.042, p = 2.73 × 10–24).
source: For example, we applied MR to further evaluate associations highlighted in our atlas with VLDL particles, where both VLDL particle average diameter size and concentration were associated with the PGS for BMI (Beta = 0.04, 95% CI = 0.033 to 0.046, p = 3.53 × 10−35 and Beta = 0.012, 95% CI = 0.006 to 0.019, p = 2.7 × 10–4, respectively) and also coronary heart disease (CHD) liability (Beta = 0.026, 95% CI = 0.019 to 0.032, p = 2.12 × 10–15 and Beta = 0.035, 95% CI = 0.028 to 0.042, p = 2.73 × 10–24, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this association with statistical details.

claim: Bidirectional MR suggested that the associations with average diameter of VLDL particles are likely attributed to a consequence of BMI and CHD liability as opposed to the size of VLDL particles having a causal influence on these outcomes.
source: Conducting bidirectional MR suggested that the associations with average diameter of VLDL particles are likely attributed to a consequence of BMI and CHD liability as opposed to the size of VLDL particles having a causal influence on these outcomes (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of bidirectional MR analysis.

claim: MR analyses suggested that the concentration of VLDL particles increases risk of CHD (Beta = 1.28 per 1-SD change in VLDL particle concentration, 95% CI = 1.25 to 1.65, p = 2.8 × 10–7).
source: In contrast, MR analyses suggested that the concentration of VLDL particles increases risk of CHD (Beta = 1.28 per 1-SD change in VLDL particle concentration, 95% CI = 1.25 to 1.65, p = 2.8 × 10–7) which may explain associations between the CHD PGS and this metabolic trait within our atlas.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the MR result with statistical details.

claim: Full GWAS summary statistics for all 249 circulating metabolic traits are available via the GWAS catalog under accession IDs GCST90092803 to GCST90093051.
source: Similar MR analyses to investigate findings from our atlas can be conducted using the full GWAS summary statistics for all 249 circulating metabolic traits available via the GWAS catalog (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/gwas/) under accession IDs GCST90092803 to GCST90093051 (Richardson et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly provides the accession IDs for the GWAS data.

claim: GlycA is a biomarker of chronic inflammation and has been found to predict various endpoints, including types of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and all-cause mortality.
source: GlycA is a biomarker of chronic inflammation and has been found to predict various endpoints, including types of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and all-cause mortality (Lawler et al., 2016; Connelly et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lawler et al., 2016 and Connelly et al., 2017.

claim: There were 44 PGS associations with GlycA which were robust to an FDR <5%.
source: There were 44 PGS associations with GlycA which were robust to an FDR <5%, used as a heuristic to determine which results to investigate in further detail (Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this finding and references Figure 2.

claim: Of the 44 PGS associated with GlycA, 36 contain one or more genetic variants that reached genome-wide significance which can be used as instrumental variables for MR.
source: Of the 44 PGS, 36 contain one or more genetic variants that reached genome-wide significance which can be used as instrumental variables for MR.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this finding.

claim: Eight exposures provided evidence of a genetically predicted effect on GlycA from MR analyses based on FDR <5%.
source: In total, eight of these exposures provided evidence of a genetically predicted effect from MR analyses based on FDR <5% (Supplementary file 1g)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this finding.

claim: BMI has a genetically predicted effect on GlycA levels (Beta = 0.16 SD increase in GlycA levels per 1 SD increase in BMI, 95% CI = 0.11 to 0.21, FDR = 1.59 × 10–8).
source: In total, eight of these exposures provided evidence of a genetically predicted effect from MR analyses based on FDR <5% (Supplementary file 1g), which included anthropometric traits such as BMI (Beta = 0.16 SD increase in GlycA levels per 1 SD increase in BMI, 95% CI = 0.11 to 0.21, FDR = 1.59 × 10–8)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this MR result with statistical details.

claim: Genetic liability to cigarettes smoked per day has a genetically predicted effect on GlycA levels (Beta = 0.27 SD change GlycA levels per 1 SD increase in cigarettes per day, 95% CI = 0.20 to 0.34, FDR = 2.84 × 10–12).
source: In total, eight of these exposures provided evidence of a genetically predicted effect from MR analyses based on FDR <5% (Supplementary file 1g), which included anthropometric traits such as BMI (Beta = 0.16 SD increase in GlycA levels per 1 SD increase in BMI, 95% CI = 0.11 to 0.21, FDR = 1.59 × 10–8) and genetic liability to cigarettes smoked per day (Beta = 0.27 SD change GlycA levels per 1 SD increase in cigarettes per day, 95% CI = 0.20 to 0.34, FDR = 2.84 × 10–12).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this MR result with statistical details.

claim: Cigarettes smoked per day was supported by both the weighted median (Beta = 0.24, 95% CI = −0.16 to 0.33, p = 2.08 × 10–8) and MR-Egger (Beta = 0.22, 95% CI = 0.07 to 0.37, p = 0.02) methods.
source: Estimates based on the IVW method were typically supported by the weighted median approach, although only cigarettes smoked per day were supported by both the weighed median (Beta = 0.24, 95% CI = −0.16 to 0.33, p = 2.08 × 10–8) and MR-Egger (Beta = 0.22, 95% CI = 0.07 to 0.37, p = 0.02) methods (Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports these MR sensitivity analysis results.

claim: A GWAS of GlycA in the UKB identified 59 independent genetic variants which were harnessed as instrumental variables (mean F = 100.1).
source: Undertaking a GWAS of GlycA in the UKB identified 59 independent genetic variants which were harnessed as instrumental variables (mean F = 100.1) (Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this finding.

claim: There was very weak evidence using the IVW method that genetically predicted GlycA has an effect on any of the 44 traits or diseases assessed based on FDR <5%.
source: In contrast to the previous analysis, we identified very weak evidence using the IVW method that genetically predicted GlycA has an effect on any of the 44 traits or diseases assessed based on FDR <5% (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this finding.

claim: The NMR signal of GlycA is a composite signal contributed by the glycan N-acetylglucosamine residues on five acute-phase proteins, including alpha1-acid glycoprotein, haptoglobin, alpha1-antitrypsin, alpha1-antichymotrypsin, and transferrin.
source: We also conducted further sensitivity analyses given that the NMR signal of GlycA is a composite signal contributed by the glycan N-acetylglucosamine residues on five acute-phase proteins, including alpha1-acid glycoprotein, haptoglobin, alpha1-antitrypsin, alpha1-antichymotrypsin, and transferrin (Otvos et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Otvos et al., 2015.

claim: Using cis-acting plasma protein and expression quantitative trait loci as instrumental variables for the five acute-phase proteins did not provide convincing evidence that they play a role in disease risk for associations between PGS and GlycA.
source: Using cis-acting plasma protein (where possible) and expression quantitative trait loci (pQTLs and eQTLs respectively) (F-stats range from 43.9 to 4468.0) as instrumental variables for these proteins (Supplementary file 1k) did not provide convincing evidence that they play a role in disease risk for associations between PGS and GlycA (Supplementary file 1l).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of these sensitivity analyses.

claim: Higher genetically predicted alpha1-antitrypsin levels have an effect on gamma glutamyl transferase levels (Beta = 0.05 SD change in GGT per 1 SD increase in protein levels, 95% CI = 0.03 to 0.07, FDR = 3.6 × 10–3).
source: The only effect estimate robust to multiple testing was found for higher genetically predicted alpha1-antitrypsin levels on gamma glutamyl transferase (GGT) levels (Beta = 0.05 SD change in GGT per 1 SD increase in protein levels, 95% CI = 0.03 to 0.07, FDR = 3.6 × 10–3)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this MR result with statistical details.

claim: The effect of alpha1-antitrypsin on GGT was not replicated when using estimates of genetic associations with GGT levels from a larger GWAS conducted in the UKB data (Beta = 1.6 × 10–3, 95% CI = −6.9 × 10–3 to 0.01, p = 0.71).
source: although this was not replicated when using estimates of genetic associations with GGT levels from a larger GWAS conducted in the UKB data (Beta = 1.6 × 10–3, 95% CI = −6.9 × 10–3 to 0.01, p = 0.71).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this replication result.

claim: Adjusting for statin therapy as a covariate or by stratification can induce collider bias.
source: However, adjusting for statin therapy as a covariate or by stratification can induce collider bias, which may be encountered when investigating the relationship between two factors (such as genetic liability towards CHD and a lipoprotein lipid metabolite) when both influence a third factor (e.g. statin therapy) (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript explains this methodological issue and references Figure 3A.

claim: Collider bias in the UKB study has been shown to distort findings.
source: In particular due to the large sample sizes provided, collider bias in the UKB study has been shown to distort findings (Griffith et al., 2020) and in extreme cases can even result in opposite conclusions being drawn (Richardson et al., 2019a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Griffith et al., 2020 and Richardson et al., 2019a.

claim: All analyses were repeated stratified by age tertiles to investigate the influence of medication use on the results.
source: Therefore, to investigate the influence of medication use on the results within our atlas, we repeated all analyses stratified by age tertiles as proposed previously (Bell et al., 2022), given that age is very unlikely to act as a collider between PGS and circulating metabolites (Figure 3B), and medication use is lower in the younger tertiles.
evidence: The manuscript describes this stratification approach with a citation to Bell et al., 2022 and references Figure 3B.

claim: In the full UKB sample there were 193 circulating metabolites associated with the PGS for CHD under a p value <0.05/19 for multiple testing correction.
source: As an example of this, in the full UKB sample there were 193 circulating metabolites associated with the PGS for CHD (constructed using genetic variants with p < 0.05 and r2 < 0.1) under a p value <0.05/19 for multiple testing correction (Supplementary file 1n).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this finding.

claim: The vast majority of metabolites associated with the CHD PGS were lipoprotein lipid traits.
source: The vast majority of these were lipoprotein lipid traits, which are likely capturing causal risk factors for CHD.
evidence: The manuscript describes the nature of the associated metabolites.

claim: Apolipoprotein B was among the top associations with the CHD PGS (Beta = 0.027, 95% CI = 0.020 to 0.033, p = 7.2 × 10–15).
source: Amongst the top associations for this PGS was apolipoprotein B (apo B) (Beta = 0.027, 95% CI = 0.020 to 0.033, p = 7.2 × 10–15)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this association with statistical details.

claim: Apolipoprotein B acts as an index of the number of circulating atherogenic lipoprotein particles.
source: Amongst the top associations for this PGS was apolipoprotein B (apo B) (Beta = 0.027, 95% CI = 0.020 to 0.033, p = 7.2 × 10–15), which acts as an index of the number of circulating atherogenic lipoprotein particles
evidence: The manuscript describes the biological role of apolipoprotein B.

claim: Apolipoprotein B has been postulated previously to be the predominating lipoprotein lipid trait indexing CHD risk.
source: which acts as an index of the number of circulating atherogenic lipoprotein particles and has been postulated previously to be the predominating lipoprotein lipid trait indexing CHD risk (Ference et al., 2019; Sniderman et al., 2019; Richardson et al., 2020b, Richardson et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ference et al., 2019, Sniderman et al., 2019, Richardson et al., 2020b, and Richardson et al., 2021.

claim: In the youngest tertile (mean age = 47.3 years, 5% statin users), the association between the CHD PGS with apo B was markedly stronger than in the total sample (Beta = 0.059, 95% CI = 0.048 to 0.070, p < 1.6 × 10–26).
source: In the youngest tertile (mean age = 47.3 years, 5% statin users), the association between the CHD PGS with apo B was markedly stronger than in the total sample (Beta = 0.059, 95% CI = 0.048 to 0.070, p < 1.6 × 10–26).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this stratified analysis result with statistical details.

claim: There was weak evidence of an inverse association between apo B and the CHD PGS in the oldest tertile (mean age = 65.3 years, 29% statin users) (Beta = −0.007, 95% CI = −0.019 to 0.004, p = 0.223).
source: In stark contrast, there was weak evidence of an inverse association between apo B and the CHD PGS in the oldest tertile (mean age = 65.3 years, 29% statin users) (Beta = −0.007, 95% CI = −0.019 to 0.004, p = 0.223), which is likely attributed to the higher proportion of participants undergoing statin therapy in this sample.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this stratified analysis result with statistical details.

claim: The inverse association between apo B and the CHD PGS in the oldest tertile is likely attributed to the higher proportion of participants undergoing statin therapy in this sample.
source: In stark contrast, there was weak evidence of an inverse association between apo B and the CHD PGS in the oldest tertile (mean age = 65.3 years, 29% statin users) (Beta = −0.007, 95% CI = −0.019 to 0.004, p = 0.223), which is likely attributed to the higher proportion of participants undergoing statin therapy in this sample.
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the finding.

claim: Concentrations of VLDL, LDL, and IDL provided evidence of a positive association with the CHD PGS in the youngest tertile.
source: Similarly, concentrations of VLDL, LDL, and IDL provided evidence of a positive association with the CHD PGS in the youngest tertile (Figure 4A)
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding and references Figure 4A.

claim: The corresponding associations between VLDL, LDL, and IDL concentrations and the CHD PGS in the oldest tertile provided weak evidence of association and in some cases reversed direction entirely.
source: whereas the corresponding associations in the oldest tertile provided weak evidence of association (and in some cases reversed direction entirely) (Figure 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding and references Figure 4.

claim: PGS were constructed excluding variants within the regions of the genome which encode the genes for 13 major regulators of NMR lipoprotein lipids signals which captured 75% of the gene–metabolite associations in the Finnish Metabolic Syndrome In Men cohort.
source: To provide insight into this issue, we constructed PGS excluding variants within the regions of the genome which encode the genes for 13 major regulators of NMR lipoprotein lipids signals which captured 75% of the gene–metabolite associations in the Finnish Metabolic Syndrome In Men (METSIM) cohort (Gallois et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript describes this sensitivity analysis approach with a citation to Gallois et al., 2019.

claim: For PGS with lipid loci excluded, anthropometric traits such as waist-to-hip ratio (N = 209), waist circumference (N = 206), and BMI (N = 205) still provided strong evidence of association with the majority of metabolic measurements on the NMR panel based on multiple testing corrections.
source: For PGS with these lipid loci excluded, anthropometric traits such as waist-to-hip ratio (N = 209), waist circumference (N = 206), and BMI (N = 205) still provided strong evidence of association with the majority of metabolic measurements on the NMR panel based on multiple testing corrections.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of this sensitivity analysis.

claim: The Alzheimer's disease PGS was associated with 60 metabolic traits robust to p < 0.05/19 in the initial analysis including lipid loci.
source: Elsewhere however, the Alzheimer's disease PGS, which was associated with 60 metabolic traits robust to p < 0.05/19 in the initial analysis including these lipid loci (Supplementary file 1q)
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this finding.

claim: The Alzheimer's disease PGS provided no convincing evidence of association with the 249 circulating metabolites after excluding the lipid loci based on p < 0.05/19.
source: provided no convincing evidence of association with the 249 circulating metabolites after excluding the lipid loci based on the same multiple testing threshold (Supplementary file 1r).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports this finding.

claim: The attenuation of evidence for Alzheimer's disease PGS associations after excluding lipid loci was likely due to variants located within the APOE locus.
source: Further inspection suggested that the likely explanation for this attenuation of evidence were due to variants located within the APOE locus (near one of the major lipid regulators APOC1) which are recognized to exert their influence on phenotypic traits via horizontally pleiotropic pathways (Ferguson et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation with a citation to Ferguson et al., 2020.

claim: Variants within the APOE locus are recognized to exert their influence on phenotypic traits via horizontally pleiotropic pathways.
